25f5e77983.q: Why does Fireworks achieve 5x performance difference compared to cloud providers running the same open source models on identical NVIDIA hardware?
25f5e77983.a: Running large language models efficiently is extremely hard. Fireworks achieves 5x performance speed and multiple times throughput difference compared to cloud providers like AWS, Azure, and GCP running the same open source models on the same NVIDIA hardware because these cloud companies pay cloud provider margins on top while Fireworks has specialized expertise in running these models efficiently. The key insight is that these companies are paying the margins of the cloud providers and running on top, making money—showing this is not a commodity pass-through business but requires deep technical expertise.

051fbeb540.q: What did AWS investor sentiment reveal about predicting long-term margin sustainability in infrastructure businesses in 2007?

If you put 30 of the smartest investors at that time in a room and asked them the probability that AWS would be a good business with durable long-term margins, Vishria estimates you would have gotten zero for 30 correct answers, even among really smart people who were around at that time.

afe900f1d4.q: How did the market size for cloud infrastructure prove wrong the 2014 narrative that AWS would consume all enterprise software opportunities?
afe900f1d4.a: By 2014, the prevailing narrative was that AWS would eat everything including databases, infrastructure, and applications due to its ability to offer services at 8% gross margin versus SaaS companies running at 85% gross margins. However, the market was so large that one vendor could not scale and consume it all. Instead, you saw Snowflake outperform Amazon Redshift, Datadog become a $100 billion company competing against AWS monitoring tools, plus Confluent, Elastic, Mongo, and Databricks all succeed. Additionally, Azure and GCP became unbelievable businesses, creating an oligopoly that now appears to be roughly 40-30-20 split, with smaller…

d8ac43f2aa.q: What does the comparison between cloud adoption timelines and current AI adoption reveal about enterprise readiness in 2025?
d8ac43f2aa.a: In 2010-2014, enterprises were super skeptical of cloud until they realized adoption was becoming a recruiting and competitive necessity. By contrast, today's enterprises are not dismissive about AI—they want it, are running experiments, spending against it, and view it as both more of an opportunity and more of a threat than they initially viewed cloud. They view AI as having more potential impact on their business, likely because they learned lessons from missing cloud adoption.

17362488bc.q: How do product managers and engineers need to work differently in the AI era compared to traditional SaaS product development?
17362488bc.a: In traditional product management, product managers understood customer problems but didn't specify implementation—that was the engineer's job. In the AI era, you must understand the jagged edge of model capabilities (what they're great at and where they fail), understand the customer problem, and bridge those gaps to build valuable solutions. You cannot do traditional product management anymore; you actually need to understand the nuances of model capabilities and put them together with customer problems. This mirrors how Cursor evolved from IDE to Tab Autocomplete to Agentic work, constantly iterating as the edge of capabilities changed.

feb393ca15.q: Why does hitting a SaaS plan destroy equity value in the AI era when it previously created it?
feb393ca15.a: For decades, the playbook was to lay out a plan, execute against it relentlessly and violently, hit your plan, and build equity value. But now the competitive frontier has completely shifted. Every day you hit that plan, you are destroying equity value because you should be pivoting toward AI opportunities. SaaS companies trading at 3x revenue today (down from 30x in 2021) are worth less even though they've grown 4x in a few years, gotten to breakeven, and hit their plans—because they haven't shifted toward what actually creates value now.

96cea03069.q: What is the core business model and technical offering of a token factory API service?
96cea03069.a: Tail Research operates as a token factory with an API where anyone can send requests to use large language models and open source language models for any task, serving tokens at unbeatable market prices. They also support agents through sale boxes, which are long-running agent virtual machines hosted in the cloud designed for agents that run for hours, days, or weeks.

5036bab6bd.q: Why is token cost the right metric to optimize for in AI inference rather than other measures?
5036bab6bd.a: Token cost is the current North Star because tokens are what the industry uses today to measure work, though the guest notes this is not the final unit of work or intelligence. After tokens, the focus will move toward outcomes, where agents self-administer token budgets depending on the task rather than companies setting monthly token budgets for engineers.

3be825ca4c.q: What market opportunity exists in serving open source language models at scale compared to proprietary closed models?
3be825ca4c.a: The rise of open source creates a robust market for customized models because customers increasingly want to own their intelligence and have control and sovereignty over it. Open source models give customers the weights and the right to deploy however they like, which cannot be taken away, making this a much more resilient market than relying on proprietary providers.

7d0174e83b.q: Why should AI inference for agents prioritize long-running background tasks over low-latency interactive responses?
7d0174e83b.a: The future of agent inference is long-horizon tasks running for hours or days at a time, where token output speed of 10 tokens per second is acceptable if it brings corresponding efficiency advantages. The best latency is no latency at all—when you wake up in the morning, the work has already been done overnight without you having to ask for it, enabling agents to operate on human timescales rather than requiring constant human prompting.

6fc95fd86e.q: What evidence supports the shift toward longer-running agents as a viable product direction?
6fc95fd86e.a: Test-time compute scaling shows that giving an agent more time produces better answers. Opus 4.5, released late last year, was the first agent suitable for longer-horizon tasks, and looking at more recent models and open source implementations, agents are now capable of running for an hour at a time, with task lengths getting longer and longer.

24b9e196be.q: What is the predicted shift in token consumption patterns between real-time and background workloads over the next several years?
24b9e196be.a: This year is expected to end at roughly 50-50 split between background and real-time workloads, but the long-term projection is 90-10 in favor of background tasks, since background processing has no human-in-the-loop constraint and can consume as many tokens as needed.

52ce691663.q: How can long-running agents improve deep research and information synthesis compared to interactive queries?
52ce691663.a: Most deep research questions benefit from analyzing 10,000 sources or more rather than just 100 or 1,000. Building authoritative indexes like one customer's parallel web systems seeks to do—indexing the whole Internet and monitoring it in real time for changes—requires the kind of exabyte-scale task that demands a very different kind and scale of intelligence.

932e92ab57.q: What role do long-running AI agents play in autonomous cybersecurity vulnerability detection?
932e92ab57.a: Rather than running an AI model once against source code, specialized agents need to be set up in actual environments where they can pen-test applications and look for multiple classes of vulnerabilities including memory errors, business logic errors, and network vulnerabilities. Security has become proof-of-work where the quality of your software security is determined by how many dollars you spend on Anthropic APIs trying to break into your software.

7b3bc22cdc.q: How does diversity in AI model capabilities improve the detection of software vulnerabilities compared to relying on a single frontier model?
7b3bc22cdc.a: The frontier of intelligence in cybersecurity is jagged—a small model might find bugs that a large model misses, Haiku finds bugs that Fable doesn't find and vice versa. This encouraged a very diverse approach to sampling and building cybersecurity agents that break software autonomously using multiple models to ensure comprehensive vulnerability detection.

e66061aa53.q: What new product categories could abundant, cheap long-running AI agents unlock for individual users?
e66061aa53.a: Proactive intelligent agents like an enhanced Siri running in the background can understand all emails and text messages received daily, building an encyclopedic view of your life to be more helpful. The machine could even understand how you interact with it and proactively surface your next action when you open your phone, with the key unlock being incredibly cheap intelligence that lets you spend tokens without any promise of return.

94f20abfa4.q: What types of problems become economically solvable with dramatically cheaper token costs for long-horizon AI tasks?
94f20abfa4.a: Intelligence can tackle any verifiable problem, which includes most software, formal math proofs, and scientific discovery. These currently have a dollar cost attached—the question is how many tokens you can harness. The cost for long-horizon tasks is now being brought within view at reasonable levels: thousands of dollars rather than millions, and potentially hundreds or tens of dollars in the near future for definitive answers to scientific questions or research problems.

e4430838d1.q: What is the three-layer technical stack approach to dramatically reducing AI inference costs?
e4430838d1.a: The master plan involves software, hardware, and power layers. On the software layer, the entire LLM stack is being built around peak GPU efficiency using NVIDIA GPUs to squeeze out more tokens from the same chip than anyone else. This starts with the lowest level of programming—kernels—where optimization can unlock significant efficiency gains.

54ffb1c893.q: What is the role of TensorCores in GPU-accelerated AI inference and how were they developed?
54ffb1c893.a: TensorCores are specialized units on the GPU that accelerate matrix multiplication. Starting in 2016, NVIDIA allocated precious silicon die area to develop the first generation of TensorCores, initially receiving only 5-10% of chip area while competing against graphics teams for silicon. The technology evolved as NVIDIA recognized that machine learning adoption of gaming GPUs was growing.

d3e5695038.q: What is NVIDIA's engineering culture principle of speed of light and how does it drive hardware optimization?
d3e5695038.a: Speed of light is NVIDIA's concept of the absolute maximum performance possible for any piece of hardware they make. The culture is deeply ingrained that if a machine can do something, engineers push it to the frontier until it reaches what's theoretically possible. It means chasing 100% speed of light—absolute numbers of what the chip can achieve—rather than relative performance versus competitors.
d3e5695038.e: Ex-NVIDIA Engineer: Why AI Is About to Get 1000x Cheaper

5e893cf566.q: Why is there a fundamental tradeoff between GPU throughput optimization and latency optimization for AI inference?
5e893cf566.a: GPUs are throughput machines happiest when given lots of work and left to chew through it at peak compute utilization, but recent AI usage pushed toward interactive chatbot tools caring about spitting answers out quickly to users. There is a classic computer science tradeoff between getting a small amount of data through the system quickly (narrow and fast) versus running wide and slow, which manifests in GPUs through batching where larger batches fill compute units but add latency per individual user request.
5e893cf566.e: Ex-NVIDIA Engineer: Why AI Is About to Get 1000x Cheaper

28346e0a38.q: How does GPU batching create a fundamental latency-throughput tradeoff for AI inference services?
28346e0a38.a: Batching groups multiple users' work together to exploit GPU parallelism, but you do net more work when running a large batch, meaning each individual token or user request spends longer on the GPU being carried with other people's traffic. This is analogous to a bus versus private transit—a bus serves many people and must work for everyone, taking a slower path with stops, while private transit takes the direct path.
28346e0a38.e: Ex-NVIDIA Engineer: Why AI Is About to Get 1000x Cheaper

3469ed4dcd.q: How does NVLink GPU interconnect technology enable distributed matrix multiplication to reduce latency?
3469ed4dcd.a: NVLink is an NVIDIA innovation that allows large matrix multiplications to be split in half and sharded across up to eight NVIDIA GPUs, with each GPU working on pieces of the larger operation and connecting their results together at the end by reducing results back together. This is an effective way to cut the minimum latency of an operation.
3469ed4dcd.e: Ex-NVIDIA Engineer: Why AI Is About to Get 1000x Cheaper

She cites Harvey's application to law as an example: recognizing that law is structured language and a good fit for language models because lawyers need to read documents and generate text from precedent. Her framework involves understanding the technology deeply from first principles rather than just evaluating customer problems in isolation.

She writes full memos (Greylock-style) and shares them with trusted investor advisors like John Lilly or Dylan Field for pushback and reflection. She emphasizes wanting people to challenge the logic rather than making decisions alone, though she notes she starts at conviction and works backwards, unlike investors who build to conviction gradually.

76f1ef1d35.q: What psychological challenges do frontier AI researchers face when working at scale in compute-intensive environments?
76f1ef1d35.a: Sarah observes that many researchers feel disempowered by the massive scale and compute requirements of frontier labs. A large contingent believes either that what they do doesn't matter because the model will do it anyway, or that only compute scale matters. She notes that if someone needs 750 billion dollars of compute spend and thousands of people are working on the problem, individual researchers feel less ownership of the outcome compared to earlier eras when smaller teams could meaningfully move the needle.

c7be54a849.q: What regulatory and infrastructure barriers are preventing rapid scaling of compute capacity for AI development?
c7be54a849.a: Sarah identifies compute availability and energy supply as critical constraints over the next five to ten years. She spoke with a hyperscaler infrastructure leader who stated nothing would move the needle at sufficient scale before 2030. She argues the bottleneck is not a technology, capability, or capitalism problem but a regulatory and alignment problem: building data centers requires convincing communities they are needed, and making nuclear power competitive requires proving safety and allowing construction of SMRs (Small Modular Reactors).

df45ccf6ed.q: What makes Tony Zhao and Cheng Chi's approach to robotics generalization and data collection particularly innovative?
df45ccf6ed.a: Sarah credits Tony Zhao and Cheng Chi at Sunday Robotics with contributing more interesting ideas in robotics over the last four years than most researchers. Their innovation is treating data scarcity as a solvable technical problem rather than a blocker. Instead of assuming they need massive internet-scale robotics datasets, they focus on being clever about collecting data in the cheapest way possible while maintaining distribution that supports real-world environments and tasks, then translating that cheap data collection into model learning.

She cites her own example of meeting an interesting company with a partner and realizing she lacked enough understanding of the science to reach conviction, so she had to step back. She contrasts this with backing exceptional people on pure pedigree grounds, but emphasizes that for most situations, an investor needs intuition on the business logic itself, not just the person.

5a56dfe391.q: What is the capital and funding timeline problem facing AI infrastructure investment compared to historical infrastructure buildouts?
5a56dfe391.a: The AI boom faces a timing mismatch: starting with free cash flow, tech companies rapidly exhausted debt markets, then Google issued equity and assembled a $500 billion fund targeting pension funds and insurance floats. 0025592c25.a: Google issued equity because once capital gets so large, companies operate in a world of absolute numbers rather than percentage numbers. Google's search business is a perfect high-margin aggregator, but the absolute profit opportunity from AI, even with lower margins, is so much larger that a smaller percentage of an astronomically larger pie results in greater absolute returns than maintaining 100 percent of a smaller business.

6f0aafb34b.q: What is the gap between AI capability in verifiable versus unverifiable domains?

44d268121e.q: Why is NVIDIA trading at its lowest forward PE in the last 10 years despite accelerating AI demand metrics?
44d268121e.a: NVIDIA is at its lowest forward PE of the last 10 years because the market believes the company is significantly over-earning. However, underlying fundamentals including GPU availability, rental pricing, spot price of DRAM, token growth, and operating cash flow from hyperscalers like Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon have all accelerated. Despite AI demand metrics showing consistent acceleration across all measured data points, the market has been selling off AI stocks due to concerns around credit financing, China's DUV capabilities, and open source model competition.

985e472235.q: What is driving GPU rental price increases despite expectations they would decline in 2024-2025?
985e472235.a: GPU prices, contrary to all 2024 and 2025 expectations, are still rising vertically in 2026. Companies signed long-term contracts expecting prices to decline slowly or precipitously, but the contracted base of installed compute is now trading at massive discounts to the current spot market. As old long-term contracts roll off and compute gets repriced higher, operating cash flow will accelerate. One startup mentioned renting Blackwell clusters at mid-$2 per GPU hour in early months and now paying just under $4 per GPU hour seven months later, representing a 50-60% increase.

f6cffee9da.q: How are hyperscaler operating cash flows accelerating despite market concerns about AI infrastructure financing?
f6cffee9da.a: Operating cash flow from Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon accelerated from 28% to 32% year-over-year, and 35% when adjusted for unusual one-time items like EU legal expenses and fines. If hyperscalers monetize new Blackwell and Rubin chip capacity at rates even modestly above Ampere (two generations behind current capability), this generates 2 trillion dollars in operating cash flow, removing 700 billion dollars of credit financing demand. This acceleration is happening right as the market focused on credit risk, suggesting the buildout can be funded primarily through operating cash flows rather than debt.
f6cffee9da.e: Why the Markets Are Pricing AI Wrong | Gavin Baker

5bc07b4a97.q: Why did the market interpret Meta's plan to rent compute capacity as negative despite no CapEx cuts?
5bc07b4a97.a: When Meta announced it would rent out compute capacity, the market interpreted this as very bearish and expected CapEx cuts. However, Meta did not cut CapEx. What actually happened was that Meta saw SpaceX sell optimized trading clusters at massive premiums to contracted rates and recognized the same opportunity. Meta's telemetry on CapEx plans showed no shift and continued getting more aggressive. Shortly after, Meta also released Llama 1.1, described as the best model in a long time, contradicting any narrative of reduced AI investment.
5bc07b4a97.e: Why the Markets Are Pricing AI Wrong | Gavin Baker

f799d351f3.q: How does open source model growth affect AI infrastructure demand and compute margins?
f799d351f3.a: Open source models like GLM 5.2 and Kimi shifted the token mix from expensive frontier model tokens with 80-95% inference margins toward open source alternatives. While this reduces margin dollars for frontier model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, it does not reduce overall compute demand because all tokens require identical amounts of computing resources. Open source effectively transfers margin dollars from frontier model providers directly to the AI infrastructure layer where cloud providers charge the same amount for compute, so total demand for infrastructure remains unchanged or increases due to the margin elasticity effect.
f799d351f3.e: Why the Markets Are Pricing AI Wrong | Gavin Baker

152eaecae5.q: What is the primary factor that would reverse the current bullish AI infrastructure outlook according to Gavin Baker?
152eaecae5.a: If operating cash flow does not continue to accelerate, that would be negative. This acceleration depends on how Anthropic, OpenAI, Grok, Cursor, and open source models perform in driving token demand growth. Additionally, if there were a sustained dramatic contraction in GPU prices making it easy to acquire GPUs, that would also be worrisome. Baker emphasized he has not heard anyone say they have too many GPUs, suggesting GPU scarcity remains a fundamental constraint.
152eaecae5.e: Why the Markets Are Pricing AI Wrong | Gavin Baker
